intents.statement: The window shows the program's own code, syntax highlighted.
Beautiful fonts: bolds, italics and ligatures.
Zoom and pan with a camera. Just the wheel, no ctrl+wheel. Smooth, never choppy, and I can pan while it zooms.
The wheel zooms everywhere, inside windows too. To scroll, drag the scrollbar.
No status bars, borders, buttons or titles that aren't needed. Middle-click closes things.
No excessive explanations in the UI. Say only what's needed, and name exact lines instead of vague labels.
All source files are laid out in space, not in one column.
Arrows show how the program is organised at the logic level: from the places in a file where they make sense, to the lines they point at.
Navigate like an IDE: definitions, usages, symbol hierarchy, collapsible blocks. Controls sit next to what they affect and appear only on hover.
Use language servers for language features instead of our own implementation.
Prose and code coexist, beautifully typeset and legible where it matters. LaTeX included.
The cursor says what will happen: a text cursor only over text I can select, the pan hand only while panning.
Chats with the agent are part of the canvas, styled like a messenger, so I don't keep a separate terminal open.
The window always shows the latest state of the code and hot reloads while the agent changes it.
The most valuable things are the sentences and decisions I make; the code is circumstantial. Every line shows the intent behind it and the agent's why, concisely, beside the code it explains.
Dark or light follows the OS theme automatically.
I can spawn an agent wherever I am and it understands that context. The prompt shows what it's about, and the camera makes room for it.
/ searches everything. ? shows every shortcut, and it should look good.
One window manager: chats, intents and explanations all obey the same rules. No special behaviour for any kind of window.
Links in chat and code are clickable, and following one brings the chat along.
Given a directory, it opens that project like an IDE would. Ctrl+O picks one. With none, it opens its own code.
It works for any codebase: TypeScript, Python, Rust, a random directory of Excel files. It's a tool, not a tech demo.
The camera has history; I can go back and forward.
Like Gource: I see each agent fly to and touch the lines it changes.
The agent can command the layout and string pieces of code together so it's clear what flows where, why and how. The pieces are views of the real code.
Esc with nothing focused shows options and settings.
Render many file types, not only text. Images first.
The window appears immediately and fills in as things load: rough layout from the filesystem first, refined as files are read.
The code stays easy to understand and reason about, and formatters and linters enforce that automatically.
Each chunk of work is committed and pushed.
The project is public with a proper README, and the repository doesn't send me noise.
Everything drawn on screen must be useful, legible and contextual: a live game-like HUD that gives immediate utility, not a static map. Arrows never just point off screen.

turns.said: what does this file do?
turns.why:
[tests/cmake_canvas_test.cpp](/home/n/code-exp-02/tests/cmake_canvas_test.cpp) is an integration test for CMake support in the source canvas application.

It creates a temporary project, launches the app, and checks that:

- Clicking filenames in `CMakeLists.txt` opens their source cards, including quoted filenames containing spaces.
- Navigation history works after following a file link.
- Hovering over a CMake command shows documentation.
- “Go to definition” finds a variable’s declaration.
- Editing `CMakeLists.txt` refreshes file links, and outdated language-server responses cannot overwrite the new links.

It simulates clicks and processes language-server messages while waiting for results. Finally, it draws the canvas and removes the temporary project.

A failed check makes the test exit with code `1`. Without an X display (`DISPLAY`), it returns `77`, which CTest treats as skipped.

turns.why:
Yes—that points to a distinction my first answer missed: **Codex’s terminal interface and its app-server don’t necessarily run the same title-generation logic.**

Your app uses app-server directly, bypassing the terminal interface. The documented naming API lets a client **set** a name with `thread/name/set` and receive `thread/name/updated`; it doesn’t promise automatic naming. [Official OpenAI documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server#api-overview)

So the likely explanation is that the terminal interface initiates title generation, while our app only listens for the result. A changing terminal-window title also doesn’t by itself establish that the saved thread name changed.

That means a preview fallback would hide the symptom. To reproduce the terminal behavior properly, we should investigate its title-generation trigger and implement the equivalent here. I haven’t yet verified that exact trigger in the installed CLI.

turns.said: investigate
turns.why:
Confirmed: **automatic naming lives in the Codex terminal interface, so our app bypasses it.**

I checked the source matching your installed CLI, **0.166.0**. Its flow is:

1. A user-message completion event arrives for an unnamed thread.
2. The terminal interface starts a hidden, ephemeral thread to generate a title of at most 36 characters.
3. It uses `gpt-5.6-luna` when available, otherwise the current model.
4. It saves the result using `thread/name/set`, provided the conversation still has no name.

Our [conversation.cpp](/home/n/code-exp-02/conversation.cpp:283) only receives name updates. It never starts that generation request or saves a generated name.

So your observation was right: the CLI actively does work that our integration is missing. Matching it requires a background title-generation request followed by `thread/name/set`; a preview fallback alone wouldn’t reproduce that behavior.

turns.said: why does the app takes so long to launch?

The biggest launch delay I measured came from decoding the repo’s demo GIFs. The app loads every file card before it opens the window, and its image loader feeds each GIF’s full contents to the decoder even though the card displays a static preview. The remaining startup work includes reading the project, syntax-highlighting and measuring every source line, uploading file cards to the GPU, and waiting for Graphviz to lay them out. Decoding only the first GIF frame would address the largest delay I observed.
